Lessons.Title: Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: write a two-variable inequality for a contextual resource budget, reason about points on and either side of a boundary line, and explain why a mathematical solution may be physically impossible. Independently authored Edulytiks material aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L22, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/22/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses landscaping decisions and specifically prioritizes hand reasoning about regions instead of graphing technology.

Independent practice context: lawn sod costs $2 per square foot, flower beds cost $12 per square foot, and the budget is at most $3,000. Let x≥0 be sod area and y≥0 flower bed area. Constraint 2x+12y≤3000. Boundary y=250−x/6, with intercepts (1500,0),(0,250). Shade below and restrict to first quadrant. A point (600,150) costs 1200+1800=3000 and lies on the included boundary.

At (600,160), spending is 1200+1920=3120, outside budget. At (1000,0), spending is 2000, within budget. Mathematical point (−600,300) satisfies −1200+3600=2400≤3000 but negative sod area has no physical meaning, so it is excluded by context despite algebraic inequality truth.

Student task: manually sketch and label the feasible first-quadrant region, classify boundary/off-boundary points, suggest a landscape allocation that uses less than full funds and another that uses exactly full funds, then critique peer claims about negative areas. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correct model, accurate region, truthful point checks and justified contextual feasibility.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cost half-plane
KeyConcepts.Definition: A total resource ceiling describes all affordable combinations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add component costs and use ≤ for a maximum.

KeyConcepts.Title: Budget boundary
KeyConcepts.Definition: Cost equality gives a straight line whose points spend exactly the limit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find intercepts by setting one area to zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical feasibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: Budget truth alone is insufficient when areas cannot be negative.
KeyConcepts.Example: (−600,300) is algebraically under budget but not physically valid.

WorkedExamples.Title: Graph the landscaping constraint
WorkedExamples.Question: Find line intercepts for 2x+12y≤3000.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: Shade below solid line within x≥0,y≥0.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Feasible region in first quadrant under/on line joining (1500,0),(0,250).

WorkedExamples.Title: Test contrasting budgets
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (600,150) feasible? Is (600,160)?
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: Nonnegative areas and exact budget make it feasible.
$3120 exceeds the budget by $120, so infeasible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject physically impossible point
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate (−600,300).
WorkedExamples.Method: Model the constraint, test boundary cases, and verify the original comparison.
Steps: As an algebraic pair, 2400≤3000 is true.
But x=−600 square feet of sod is physically meaningless.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Mathematically meets cost inequality but is not a valid landscaping plan.
WorkedExamples.Check: The nonnegative-area constraint is independent of cost.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Graphing the cost inequality over negative-area quadrants as physically feasible
Using technology instead of reasoning about the region in this lesson
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source lesson explicitly focuses on manual half-plane reasoning.

SummaryPoints: A resource inequality yields a half-plane bounded by a related equality.
Only nonnegative areas are physically meaningful in landscaping.
An inclusive budget includes exact-boundary allocations.
Teacher scores original graph, point checks and context explanation.
